title: Anthropogenic and climatic factors regulate algal bloom intensity and timing in global lakes under climate change
abstract: Algal blooms are becoming more frequent and intense in lakes worldwide, but how bloom intensity and timing co-vary at the global scale is unclear. Here we analyze two decades of Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer satellite observations for 4085 lakes ( > 20 square kilometres) to compare changes in intensity (fractional floating algal cover) and timing (start and end dates) of surface algal bloom. We find that intensity and timing often change independently: about 71% of lakes show increasing intensity, mainly associated with higher population density and agricultural pressure, whereas temperature and wind better explain shifts in bloom timing, especially in cold regions. Under a medium-emission scenario, tropical lakes show rapid intensification with modest timing shifts, while cold-region lakes exhibit regionally contrasting timing changes. This decoupling may alter lake food webs and carbon cycling, underscoring the need for region-specific management strategies under climate change. Population density and agricultural activity intensify fractional floating algal cover in 71% global lakes, whereas temperature and wind regulate the bloom phenology, according to an analysis of Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) data across 4085 global lakes for two decades.
problem: It is unclear how algal bloom intensity and timing co-vary at a global scale, and the spatial patterns, long-term trends, and governing factors of bloom phenology across the world's lakes remain poorly characterized, hindering predictions of ecosystem responses to climate change.
method: This study derives fractional floating algae cover from MODIS satellite imagery for 4,085 global lakes using a nonlinear unmixing model, applies a Fourier-fitted threshold method to extract bloom timing, and uses principal component regression to project future changes under different climate scenarios.
task: The task is to analyze historical trends, identify the anthropogenic and climatic drivers of algal bloom intensity and timing in global lakes using satellite data, and project their future changes under different climate scenarios.
innovation: Using two decades of satellite data across 4,085 global lakes, this study reveals that algal bloom intensity and timing are regulated by different drivers, with anthropogenic pressures controlling intensity and climatic factors governing timing, indicating a global-scale decoupling of these phenomena.

Climate forcing datasets from the ISIMIP were downloaded to simulate the response of algal blooms to climate change 68. The ISIMIP3b is dedicated to quantifying climate-related risks at different levels of global warming and socioeconomic change. The dataset includes historical (1850–2014) and future (2015-2100) conditions on the basis of bias adjustment and statistical downscaling to a 0.5- degree horizontal resolution of Phase 6 Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) daily output from MRI-ESM2-0 via ISIMIP3BASD v2.5.0 and W5E5 v2.0. The variables we used included the near-surface air temperature (TEM), near-surface wind speed (WIN), and precipitation (PRE) under three emission scenarios (SSP 1-2.6, SSP 2-4.5, SSP 4-6.0). They were used in driving analysis and future changes of algal bloom phenology.

(1) Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) surface reflectance data. The MODIS Aqua surface reflectance products (MYD09GA.061 and MYD09GQ.061) from 2003 to 2022 were integrated into the Google Earth Engine 63. The MYD09GA dataset provides mapped daily surface spectral reflectance at 500 m in 7 bands (469, 555, 645, 859, 1,240, 1,640, and 2,130 nm) ranging from the visible to the shortwave infrared (SWIR) wavelengths. MYD09GQ includes two bands centered at 645 and 859 nm with a 250-m spatial resolution, which are used to replace the corresponding bands in MYD09GA to improve the spatial resolution.

(2) Landsat 8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) satellite data. The Landsat 8 OLI/TIRS Collection 2 atmospherically corrected surface reflectance data 64 are available from the Google Earth Engine. The Landsat 8 OLI data exhibit a temporal resolution of 16 days and a spatial resolution of 30 m and encompass 5 visible and near-infrared (NIR) bands and 2 SWIR bands. These data were regarded as reference data for developing the FAC model in this study.

Global pattern and long-term trend of the algal bloom phenology
Satellite-based algal bloom phenology was generated (Supplementary Figures 3 and 4) to determine the spatial and temporal patterns of the algal bloom phenology in 4085 lakes with areas > 20 km² worldwide (Fig. 1). Because FAC is derived from surface reflectance, it is particularly sensitive to dense, surface-accumulating blooms. Such blooms are most commonly associated with buoyant cyanobacteria, whereas subsurface blooms formed by non-buoyant phytoplankton groups (e.g., diatoms) are less effectively detected. The global mean FAC across all lakes is 1.69 ± 1.08%. The six continents exhibit variations in mean FAC values, with Oceania demonstrating the highest value of 2.57 ± 2.40% (N = 24) and Asia exhibiting the lowest value of 1.48 ± 1.02% (N = 501) (Fig. 1b). There are 134 lakes with mean FAC > 5%, which are primarily North American lakes smaller than 100 km² (N = 89, accounting for 66.5%). The peak FAC in the Northern Hemisphere occurred around day of the year (DOY) 199 (mean FAC = 2.82 ± 2.49%), whereas the peak FAC in the Southern Hemisphere occurred around DOY 355 (mean FAC = 3.43 ± 4.26%) (Fig. 1e). In addition, the SOD and EOD exhibit substantial variations across the geographical regions and climate zones (Figs. 1d-1h). Africa exhibited the earliest average SOD (71.89), whereas North America exhibited the latest average SOD (132.47) (Fig. 1g).
